messages.subject: Marine mammal distance sampling survey - replication/increasing
messages.subject_clean: Marine mammal distance sampling survey - replication/increasing
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was hoping for some feedback re increasing the number of transects for =
a marine mammal survey.

My study area is ~75 km by 40 km. The transects will be spaced 6 km apart=
 (based on previous research indicating a truncation distance of ~2-3 km =
for humpback whales). Thus, the maximum number of transects I can fit in =
my study area in one survey pass is 12 transects. However, distance sampl=
ing literature states it is best to have at least 20 transects.

Can I increase the number of transects by using Distance to create a surv=
ey design that randomly places transects 6km apart, and repeating this pr=
ocess 3 times? i.e. within one season, survey the study area 3 complete t=
imes using three different sets of randomly placed transects, resulting i=
n a sample size of 36 transects?
Or, generating a survey design with randomly placed transects in Distance=
 once, and for the subsequent two survey passes, offsetting the transects=
 by 2km each?

Which option is best? Three random survey designs or three survey passes =
of transects offset by 2km from the original random survey design (to inc=
rease survey coverage of the study area)?
Can these data then be analyzed as 36 independent samples?

This survey will be conducted each season over 1 year (4 seasons of data =
total). I was planning on surveying the same transects across seasons and=
 potentially pooling the data as suggested in previous posts (i.e. sample=
 size is 36, and length =3D line length x number of visits).
I hope this makes sense and any feedback would be much appreciated.

Please reply to my e-mail address below; I will summarize the ensuing dis=
cussion
to the list.

Thanks, Elaine Leung
elaine...@gmail.com

--

messages.subject: Re: Marine mammal distance sampling survey -
messages.body_plain:
Here is the summary of advice from Eric Rexstad in response to my earlier=
 post:

1:  I think your 2km systematic offset surveyed a couple of times during =
the season is probably fine.  Better than random selection because being =

systematic ensures even coverage throughout the study area.

2:  Once you have transitted through your study area on your 12 transects=

, your ship needs to get back to port.  Could you not return along your "=
offset" transects?

3:  There is no necessity for your transects to run the full 40km width o=
f your study area.  You could use "segmented transects" using the term us=
ed in the Distance survey design engine.  It has the disadvantage of havi=

ng "off-effort" in your study area.

--

messages.subject: Re: Marine mammal distance sampling survey -
messages.body_plain:
Dear Elaine,

Something else that also comes to mind here is that if you are sampling=20
the entirety of the sampling area you need to be careful. This is an=20
issue that tends to be ignored and that was alluded to by

Cassey, P. & Mcardle, B. An assessment of distance sampling techniques=20
for estimating animal abundance Environmetrics, 1999, 10, 261-278

which refer in their abstract that

"If the proportion of the study area surveyed by transects is large=20
however, then the presence of large between PSU variation will cause the=20
variance estimates from program DISTANCE to be a sizeable overestimate."

If I recall correctly there is also something on this on the=20
introduction to distance sampling 2001 book, but I don't have my copy=20
with me.

The issue is that the conventional estimation of the encounter rate=20
available in Distance assumes that one uses a "small" number of=20
transects of the available sampling units (in theory, there would be an=20
infinite number of sampling units). In the limit, if you sample the=20
entire area of inference, there is no encounter rate variance, the only=20
variance that exists is from the detection probability (assuming no=20
individuals, not clusters). However, if you input the data into Distance=20
ignoring this, the software assumes these were a random sample of=20
transects and assumes that the variance is valid. It's like comparing=20
variance estimates in a finite population in which (1) you account or=20
(2) you don't account for the fact that the population is finite. If the=20
population is finite, and you sample a large proportion of the available=20
sampling units, you can massively overestimate variance if you ignore=20
the finite population correction factor.

The above is only considering spatial variability, and assuming a single=20
sampling event. If you have also temporal variability to care for (i.e.=20
you have a sample of days over a year, but you want inferences about the=20
average density over that year) then things can become less clear,=20
because given that animals can go in and out of your study area during=20
the period of interest, then even covering the entire area you still=20
have (temporal) variability associated with your data. You need to think=20
carefully what is the variability you are interested in (spatial,=20
temporal or both).

Given how you described your study area, I wonder if this is worth=20
considering. I hope this has not made it more confusing than you'd hope f=
or.

cheers,

Tiago

messages.subject: Encounter Rate Variance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

The dataset I am working with comes from a four year study looking at
changes in bird densities over time on a restoration site and a reference
site.  One line transect on the restoration site that was ~1 km in length
was repeatedly surveyed over the study period (once per week during the
non-breeding season and once every other week during the non-breeding
season) and two line transects on the reference site of approximately equal
length were repeatedly surveyed on the same schedule as the reference
site.

When I analyzed my data I pooled all observations with sufficient numbers
of observations and treated them as two samples for each species (pre and
post restoration) regardless of detection method (song, call or visual).
For example, all pre-restoration Marsh Wren observations were analyzed as a
sample and all post restoration Marsh Wren observations were analyzed as a
sample.

When I analyzed the data I got an error message saying: "** Warning: Cannot
estimate encounter rate variance empirically as there is only one sample.
Setting encounter rate variance to zero. **".  Is it ok to have my
encounter rate variance be zero and still get an accurate estimate of
density?

Also, I had a committee member question my pooling of observations because
of territoriality of some species.  He was concerned that if the site was
surveyed repeatedly on the same transect I might be picking up the same
individual birds each time that had breeding territories that overlapped
the transect.  Would these territorial individual songbirds that were
detected multiple times over the study period bias my estimate of density?
If so, is there a way to correct for the bias?

Thanks in advance for input.

-Ben
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Ben Wishnek, Master's of Science Degree Candidate
Oregon State University
Environmental Sciences Graduate Program
104 Wilkinson Hall
Corvallis, OR  97331

messages.subject: Re: Encounter Rate Variance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben, List,

What Distance is telling you is that there is no good way to estimate=20
the variance on the encounter rate component, so Distance cannot=20
reliably get a variance for your density estimate. This has been covered=20
in previous posts I suspect. Note that you should not get fooled by the=20
fact that for the reference site you don't get a warning. You only have=20
two lines there, and so, while Distance can actually compute a variance,=20
that variance is totally unreliable. Typically you want a reasonable=20
number of transects for each density (and corresponding variance)=20
estimate, and 12 - 15 is a minimum number people usually recommend (I do=20
not have my IDS book here to get the right number...).

If I understand correctly you have something like a BACI design, with=20
samples from pre-and post restoration in a control and a restored site?=20
I would not have used just a single line (or a couple), because that=20
precludes access to spatial variation which is certainly important, but=20
given you have, I guess you could still use your weekly visits to get a=20
temporal variance, and hence allow you to see whether differences before=20
and after the restoration are statistically significant. This would be=20
valid for your lines, not for the wider area.

As for the concerns regarding territorial species, it is true that you=20
might be getting the same birds consistently every week, but then again,=20
there's nothing wrong about that per se. That is what you get. Density=20
estimates will be valid for that line alone. So there's no bias involved=20
(all else being fine). Assume birds are territorial, and no change in=20
density over time. Each week you are estimating the same density. Some=20
days you see more, some days less, due to randomness in the birds activit=
y.

Remember the perhaps obvious: when you pool all data, you have to=20
account for the number of survey days to get a mean density estimate for=20
that line. That might be dealt directly by Distance depending how you=20
have input the data (e.g. if you have used 4 strata, with each visit to=20
a transect as a separate line transect, but I suspect you did not do=20
this. maybe you simply have added up the line lengths, i.e., say you had=20
40 weekly visits, then effort was recorded as 40 km). But if weekly=20
visits are lines in Distance, then the variance associated with the=20
weekly counts is temporal, not spatial, so strictly  inferences are not=20
valid for the wider area.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Announce: Distance 6.2 Release 1
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance-sampling list,

We are pleased to announce the release of a new version of Distance, version
6.2.  Copies are available at the Distance web site
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

A summary of changes relative to Distance 6.0 is given below.  We recommend all
users of Distance 6.0 update to the new version.

Best wishes,

  - Len Thomas

New in Distance 6.2

Multiple bug fixes and minor enhancements, as summarized below.

CDS/MCDS Engine
- An important bug that meant variance estimates for point transects were
incorrect has been fixed - please re-run all point transect analyses from
Distance 6.0 and 6.1
- Other minor improvements in output labeling

MRDS Engine
- R package mrds updated to 2.1.5 (compiled with R 3.1.0)
- Multiple other changes and bug fixes -- see NEWS file of R package mrds
- Monotonicity checks now performed in ds models
- Left truncation for exact and interval data now possible in interface

DSM Engine
- R package dsm updated to 2.2.3 (compiled with R 3.1.0)
- Some added features: autocorrelation plots, gam.check fitting diagnostics
- Regarding diagnostic output, shows diagnostic plots from rqgam.check (which
uses randomized quantile residuals (Dunn and Smyth 1996)) rather than gam.check.
  Also displays the text output from gam.check, which it did not before.
- For other changes to the R package, see NEWS file of R package dsm
- Some minor changes to properties pages:
  + Some options dropped - ability to control the weights; ability to specify a
table of detectablity values; ability to set an overdispersion value
  + Multiple changes to the density surface tab of dsm engine
  + No need to specify a tilda when writing out the DS model in Density Surface
| DS Model | Formula.
  + Changed the header in the results details of the component smooth plots from
"Diagnostic-plot" to "Component smooth".  Better describes what they are.  (Plot
files are also renamed from diag... to smooth...)

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

              email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
Distance home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

messages.subject: AIC in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I have a question regarding model selection using the MRDS engine.

=46rom my reading of the literature, I understand that point independence=
 (PI) models often tend to outperform, and be selected against, their ful=
l independence (FI) equivalent. This was the case for example in the golf=
 tee survey described in the advanced book, or in a survey of crabeater s=
eals undertaken by Borchers et al. (2006) - Accommodating unmodeled heter=
ogeneity in double-observer distance sampling surveys, Biometrics 62(2):3=
72-8.

I have been analysing aerial survey data for bottlenose dolphins using MR=
DS, and, contrary to the above scenario, all my FI models have a lower AI=
C value than their correspond PI form.

In a previous post to the list (dated 8th March 2010), Jeff Laake wrote t=
hat he rarely saw real examples in which PI was not favored over FI. I ta=
ke from this that, although unusual, this situation can still occur (and =
is not necessarily the sign of an analysis gone wrong?).=20

I have been scratching my head to find a plausible explanation for these =
results, and the only reasoning I could come up with is that (1) I have a=
 very narrow survey strip (w=3D450 m), so there likely isn't much room fo=
r unmodelled heterogeneity away from the trackline, especially once covar=
iates are added into the models, and (2) PI models are effectively more c=
otsly to fit than FI models on small datasets like mine (n =3D 36 sightin=
gs) (as they require the estimation of more parameters - some for the CDS=
 component, and some for the MRDS component) ...?

Has anyone else obtained lower AIC scores in FI models compared to PI mod=
els?
I would appreciate your thoughts/comments on the topic.

Thanks in advance -- Phil

--

messages.subject: Re: AIC in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Below are the responses I received. Many warm thanks to Jeff and Brett fo=
r their prompt feedback.

Brett Collier ----

I suspect that Jeff will respond to you in the near term as he is the exp=
ert on this, but I think that your diagnosis, based off of your email, if=
 fairly accurate in that you have a fairly narrow strip so perhaps the di=
stance heterogeneity does not come into play.  We had the same issue with=
 some avian point count surveys where their was no difference between FI =
and PI (see link below), which was probably a result of 1) not enough dis=
tance bins and 2) fairly high detectability in the 2 bins when the birds =
call.

http://irnr.tamu.edu/bret/BretWebSiteDocs/CollierLF2013.pdf

For what its worth, it 'can' happen, but when it does it is typically bec=
ause we constrained the system in such a way that the distance effects ar=
e not yet being observed, such as in the 2 bin bird point count case wher=
e I saw the same thing.

Jeff Laake -----

FI was the best model in Buckland et al. (2010) in Biometrics for the min=
ke whale data.  Your reasoning is sound and while PI is the most common o=
utcome it is not the only possible outcome.

Cheers -- Phil

--
